claim: The transmembrane domain of the TRP channel adopts a structure that is remarkably similar to voltage-activated potassium channels.
source: Structures of TRPV1 have been solved by cryo-electron microscopy (EM) (Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013) (Figure 1A), revealing that the transmembrane domain of the TRP channel adopts a structure that is remarkably similar to voltage-activated potassium channels (Long et al., 2007), as well inositol trisphosphate and ryanodine receptors (Yan et al., 2015; Zalk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Long et al., 2007

claim: Protons activate TRPV1 from the external side of the pore.

claim: Only the full-length TRPV1 channel binds RTx with high affinity.
source: Although we succeeded in producing truncated constructs of TRPV1, only the full-length channel binds RTx with high affinity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F

claim: Full-length TRPV1 channel displayed saturable 3H-RTx binding to intact cells, with a Kd of 7.0 nM.
source: Although protein levels were comparable for these constructs based on GFP fluorescence, only the full-length TRPV1 channel displayed saturable 3H-RTx binding to intact cells, with a Kd of 7.0 nM (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The Y511A mutant greatly diminished RTx binding to GFP-tagged TRPV1.
source: To demonstrate that only the full-length GFP-tagged channel presents specific high-affinity binding to RTx, we studied the Y511A mutant that disrupts vanilloid binding (Jordt and Julius, 2002; Yang et al., 2015), and found that the mutant greatly diminished RTx binding to GFP-tagged TRPV1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and citations to Jordt and Julius, 2002; Yang et al., 2015

claim: RTx bound to His-tagged TRPV1 construct with an affinity that was comparable to that observed with GFP-tagged TRPV1.
source: We also measured the binding of RTx to a His-tagged TRPV1 construct and observed that RTx bound with an affinity that was comparable to that observed with GFP-tagged TRPV1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: DkTx binding can enhance the affinity of TRPV1 for RTx.
source: We therefore tested whether binding of DkTx can enhance the affinity of TRPV1 for RTx, which would be predicted by an allosteric model wherein the two activators promote opening by binding more tightly to the open state.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The Kd for RTx binding to 1D4-tagged TRPV1 is 0.6 nM under control conditions.
source: Under these conditions, we measured a Kd for RTx binding to 1D4-tagged TRPV1 of 0.6 nM under control conditions, about ten fold higher affinity than what we measured in intact cells using GFP-tagged TRPV1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: DkTx enhanced the affinity for RTx by about 3-fold.
source: When we measured the concentration-dependence of RTx binding to 1D4-tagged TRPV1 in the presence of DkTx, we observed that the tarantula toxin enhanced the affinity for RTx by about 3-fold (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The effects of DkTx on RTx binding were concentration-dependent.
source: The effects of DkTx were concentration-dependent (Figure 2B) and were observed independent of whether the binding assay was performed at 37°C (our standard temperature) or at 30°C (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: DkTx binds to the preparation of TRPV1.

evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing DkTx effects on RTx binding

claim: Binding of DkTx and RTx are allosterically coupled.

evidence: Supported by experimental data showing DkTx enhances RTx binding affinity

claim: S512 (F472 in TRPV2) is a potentially important determinant of RTx binding to TRPV1.

evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citations to Elokely et al., 2016; Gavva et al., 2004; Jordt and Julius, 2002; Yang et al., 2015

claim: The S512F mutant speeds RTx dissociation.
source: Similar results were obtained with each of the four TRPV1 mutants (Figure 3B–E), with the exception being the S512F mutant, where we could readily see dissociation of RTx after removing the vanilloid from the recording chamber (Figure 3B), suggesting that this mutant weakens the affinity of RTx.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Individual substitution of S512, M547, T550, or E570 by the equivalent residues in TRPV2 is not sufficient to produce large disruptions in the activation by a saturating concentration of RTx.
source: Although previous studies suggest that some of these residues are determinants of vanilloid-sensitivity in TRPV1 (Gavva et al., 2004; Jordt and Julius, 2002; Yang et al., 2015), their individual substitution by the equivalent residues in TRPV2 is not sufficient to produce large disruptions in the activation by a saturating concentration of RTx.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-E and citations to Gavva et al., 2004; Jordt and Julius, 2002; Yang et al., 2015

claim: The TRPV1 quadruple mutant (S512F, M547L, T550L, E570Q) completely lost sensitivity to RTx while retaining sensitivity to 2-APB.
source: We next combined all four mutants to make a quadruple mutant (TRPV1 QM), which completely lost sensitivity to RTx while retaining sensitivity to 2-APB (Figure 4A), suggesting that differences between TRPV1 and TRPV2 at some or all of these positions can explain the differential sensitivity of the two TRP channels to RTx.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Both S512F/M547L and S512F/T550L channels lost sensitivity to RTx.
source: Both S512F/M547L and S512F/T550L channels lost sensitivity to RTx, whereas the S512F/E570Q mutant retained RTx sensitivity (Figure 4B–D), indicating that S512, M547 and T550 are more important determinants of TRPV1 activation by RTx than E570.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: The S512F/E570Q mutant retained RTx sensitivity.
source: Both S512F/M547L and S512F/T550L channels lost sensitivity to RTx, whereas the S512F/E570Q mutant retained RTx sensitivity (Figure 4B–D), indicating that S512, M547 and T550 are more important determinants of TRPV1 activation by RTx than E570.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: S512, M547 and T550 are more important determinants of TRPV1 activation by RTx than E570.

evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on double mutants shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: Only the triple mutant that left S512 intact retained sensitivity to RTx.
source: We also examined all four possible triple mutants, and only the mutant that left S512 intact retained sensitivity to RTx (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: S512 is the most critical determinant of RTx sensitivity.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that 1) S512 is the most critical determinant of RTx sensitivity, 2) M547 and T550 are also important, and 3) E570 may or may not contribute to the differential sensitivity of TRPV1 and TRPV2 to RTx.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on single, double, triple, and quadruple mutants

claim: TRPV2 is completely insensitive to RTx.

claim: TRPV2 QM (F472S, L507M, L510T, Q530E) was robustly activated by RTx.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: TRPV2 QM remained insensitive to capsaicin.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: RTx produced much stronger activation of TRPV2 QM when compared to 2-APB.
source: RTx produced much stronger activation when compared to 2-APB, and we observed little evidence for dissociation of the vanilloid after its removal from the recording chamber (Figure 5B), suggestive of strong and stable binding to TRPV2 QM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Little evidence for dissociation of RTx from TRPV2 QM was observed after its removal from the recording chamber.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The TRPV2 QM displayed robust and high-affinity RTx binding with a Kd of 18 nM.

claim: The affinity of RTx for the TRPV2 QM is about 30-fold lower compared to TRPV1.

claim: The triple mutant that retained F472 was insensitive to RTx.

claim: Either L507M or L510T rendered the TRPV2 channel sensitive to RTx when combined with F472S.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Only two point mutations are required to make the TRPV2 channel sensitive to RTx.
source: We also investigated the RTx sensitivity of three double mutants containing the F472S mutation, and observed that either L507M or L510T rendered the TRPV2 channel sensitive to RTx (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), again matching our results for loss of function experiments in TRPV1 and demonstrating that only two point mutations are required to make the TRPV2 channel sensitive to RTx.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The F472S single mutation is likely not sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to TRPV2.
source: Notably, the F472S single mutation is likely not sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to TRPV2, as the F472S/Q530E was unresponsive to the vanilloid (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: This is the first direct biochemical demonstration of allosteric coupling between two ligands that activate TRPV1.

claim: As few as two TRPV1 residues need to be introduced into TRPV2 in order for RTx to bind to the channel with high affinity and to fully activate the channel.

Our results demonstrate that as few as two TRPV1 residues need to be introduced into TRPV2 in order for RTx to bind to the channel with high affinity and to fully activate the channel (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 6).

claim: A quiescent RTx binding pocket already exists in TRPV2.

evidence: Inferred from the finding that only two mutations are needed to confer RTx sensitivity

claim: The native F472 in TRPV2 (corresponding to S512) would likely sterically clash with the methoxyl and hydroxyl groups of RTx.
